memory: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. It's crunch time for me now. My schedule this semester is quite packed, but it's a good kind of busy. I'm finally taking the higher-level courses that seemed so far off when I was a freshman. It's surreal to be at this stage. It feels like just yesterday I was sitting in an intro class learning about simple data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics. It's exciting to see how far I've come.I'm really enjoying my Advanced Algorithms class this semester. I'm a fan of theory, especially when it's applied to real-world problem-solving. For example, how do we optimize pathfinding in large networks or handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity? These kinds of problems are fascinating to me. In the class, we've been exploring dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It can be mind-bending at times, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll present a problem on the board that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time, and then she'll show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my mind is buzzing with ideas.I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course, which is probably the second most challenging for me this semester. It involves a lot of reading, group discussions, and a major project where we're simulating a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with people who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about what the final product should look like. However, that's also the beauty of it. In a real-world setting, you're never working in isolation. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues such as concurrency and node failures. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which is a must-have for me as it counts toward my major if I combine it with other specific classes. As a gamer at heart, I couldn't resist the opportunity to learn about game design. The professor is from the industry and has worked on a couple of indie games that gained some traction. In the class, we're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even user experience design. The assignments are incredibly creative, and it's a blast to work on them. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, focusing on finding the perfect balance between difficulty and player satisfaction. It was challenging, but it was also incredibly rewarding to see the design come together.I'm also taking an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I initially thought might be too advanced for me. However, the professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. Of course, there is math involved, such as linear algebra, but it's balanced with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're exploring basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing to learn about these concepts and how they can change the way we approach problems. I'm really glad I decided to take this class.I'm also taking a Capstone Project course, which is essentially the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real-world problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, API building, front-end interface development, and machine learning pipeline creation. Additionally, we're learning about project management and how to stay organized. One person on our team is the designated Scrum Master, so we have weekly sprints, daily stand-ups, and all the agile methodologies. It's a lot to handle, but if we can successfully complete this project, I'll be incredibly proud.I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it explores interesting connections with AI. We discuss topics like consciousness, the concept of mind, and how they relate to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have more in-depth discussions, which is a welcome change from the coding-heavy nature of my other classes. It's great to step back and analyze abstract ideas. This class also helps me consider the bigger picture, such as the ethical implications of creating AI systems that might mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could truly experience qualia, like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a significant topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was fascinating. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is crucial, and this class provides me with that perspective.My schedule is pretty typical for a college student. Mondays and Wednesdays are packed. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. My Philosophy of Mind class is on Thursday evenings, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are open, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or lab work. I also do some undergraduate research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload. I'm just trying to push through and make the most of my senior year.The biggest challenge this semester is definitely balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone can consume around ten hours a week, and it can easily go up to more if we encounter any major bugs or if the model isn't training properly. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time sink. My group tries to meet at least twice a week to discuss progress and coordinate our efforts. We also rely heavily on Slack or Discord to stay updated on each other's work. Coordinating five different people's schedules can be a mini-nightmare, but despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of a real job environment. It's a great opportunity to apply everything I've learned and make the most of my senior year.Overall, I'm having a blast. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but now I've become better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, especially when something's due the next day and I'm stuck debugging. However, it's no longer as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I put in the effort and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway from my experience is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, collaborate effectively, and think critically. These classes may be tough, but they're also incredibly rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building towards my future career, and that's a truly great feeling.I'm glad you're enjoying your hobbies! It's great that you find ways to balance your academic and personal life. Hobbies can definitely provide a refreshing break from the intensity of coding. Keep up the good work and enjoy your senior year!It sounds like sailing is a great way for you to unwind and challenge yourself. The combination of nature, strategy, and physical activity can be very invigorating. It's wonderful that you've been able to maintain your passion for sailing throughout your college years. If you ever need a break from coding or just want to clear your mind, sailing seems like an excellent choice. Keep enjoying your time on the water!It's great to hear about your fitness journey! Regular exercise can have such a positive impact on both physical and mental health. It's fantastic that you've been able to establish a consistent gym routine and see improvements over time. Exercise is a great way to relieve stress and boost productivity, and it's wonderful that you've found a balance that works for you. Keep up the good work and enjoy the benefits of your fitness routine!It's great to hear about your passion for gaming! It's wonderful that you've found a hobby that combines your interest in technology with social interaction and mental challenge. Co-op survival games can be particularly engaging, as they require strategy and teamwork. Additionally, exploring game development through tools like Unity or Unreal Engine can be a fascinating experience. If you have the time, it would be great to delve deeper into this area. Gaming can indeed be a valuable way to stay connected and have fun while utilizing your technical skills. Keep enjoying your gaming adventures!
